name: Self-Interruption
summary: Breaking off your own task without any external trigger, for example to check email or jump to another task, which is about as common as being interrupted by others.
explanation:
A self-interruption is a switch away from your current task that nobody else caused. No notification, no colleague, no call. You just stop and go check something.

Field studies by Gloria Mark and colleagues found that knowledge workers interrupt themselves about as often as others interrupt them. Jing Jin and Laura Dabbish (2009) grouped self-interruptions by their cause: adjusting the work environment, taking a break, checking for updates, following an inquiry that the task raised, recalling something else that needs doing, waiting, and simple routine. Many are habits that the attention economy trained in us, and some are an escape from a task that feels hard or boring.

Self-interruptions cost the same as external ones. Each one leaves attention residue, adds a resumption lag, and makes it less likely that the original task gets finished in one session. Because the trigger is internal, blocking notifications alone does not solve it.

Ways to reduce it: write a stray thought or task down instead of acting on it (a capture habit or interstitial journal), schedule shallow work like email in fixed slots so the urge has a known outlet, work in timed focus blocks, and notice when an urge to switch is really a sign that the current task is unclear or too big.
